title: Of solitude
paragraphs: Let us set aside that long comparison between the active and the solitary life; and as for the fine sayings with which ambition and greed disguise their vices — that we are not born for ourselves but for the public — let us boldly turn to those who are actually in public affairs. Let them lay their hands on their hearts and then say whether, on the contrary, they don't seek titles and offices and the world's tumult precisely to make their private advantage at public expense. The corrupt routes by which, in our time, they reach the height their ambition aims at make it clear enough that their ends cannot be very good. Let us tell ambition that she herself is what gives us a taste for solitude — for what does she avoid so much as company? What does she seek so much as elbow room? A man can live well or badly anywhere; but if what Bias says is true, that the greater part is the worse part, or what Ecclesiastes says, that there is not one good man in a thousand:
"Rari quippe boni: numero vix sunt totidem quot Thebarum portae, vel divitis ostia Nili,"
["Good men are rare: there are barely as many as the gates of Thebes or the mouths of the rich Nile." — Juvenal, Sat., xiii. 26.]

the contagion is very dangerous in a crowd. A man must either imitate the vicious or hate them — both dangerous, either to resemble them because they are many or to hate many because they are different from us. Merchants who go to sea are right to be careful that those they sail with are not dissolute blasphemers or otherwise vicious; they regard such company as unlucky. That is why Bias said, with a smile, to those who, caught in a dangerous storm with him, were calling on the gods: "Hush, speak softly, so they may not know you are here in my company." And, more telling still, Albuquerque, viceroy in the Indies for King Emmanuel of Portugal, in an extreme peril of shipwreck, took a young boy upon his shoulders for this sole reason: that in the shared danger the boy's innocence might serve to recommend him to the divine favour and bring them safe to shore. It isn't that a wise man cannot live contented anywhere and be alone even in the middle of a palace crowd; but if it is left to his choice, the schoolman will tell you he should flee the very sight of the crowd. He will put up with it if he must; but if it is up to him, he will choose to be alone. He cannot think himself sufficiently free of vice if he still has to contend with it in other men. Charondas punished as evildoers those convicted of keeping bad company. There is nothing so unsociable and so sociable as man — the one through his vice, the other through his nature. And Antisthenes, in my view, did not give a good enough answer when someone reproached him for frequenting bad company by saying that doctors live well enough among the sick — for if doctors contribute to the patients' health, they cannot help, through contagion, constant exposure to disease, and familiarity with it, impairing their own.

Now the aim, I take it, is one and the same: to live more at leisure, more at our ease. But people do not always go the right way about it. They often think they have given up business entirely when they have only swapped one occupation for another. Running a private household is hardly less trouble than running a kingdom. Wherever the mind is troubled, it is wholly disordered, and domestic concerns are no less wearing for being less important. Besides, having shaken off the court and the marketplace, we have not shaken off the principal vexations of life:
"Ratio et prudentia curas, Non locus effusi late maris arbiter, aufert;"
["Reason and prudence, not a place commanding a view of the wide sea, take cares away." — Horace, Ep., i. 2.]
ambition, greed, indecision, fear, and unruly desires do not leave us just because we leave our native country:
"Et Post equitem sedet atra cura;"
["And black care sits behind the rider." — Horace, Od., iii. 1, 40].
they often follow us right into cloisters and philosophical schools; no desert, no cave, no hair shirt, no fast can shake us free of them:
"Haeret lateri lethalis arundo."
["The fatal shaft sticks fast in her side." — Aeneid, iv. 73.]
Someone telling Socrates that a certain person was no better for all his travels: "I quite believe it," said Socrates, "for he took himself along."
"Quid terras alio calentes Sole mutamus? patriae quis exsul Se quoque fugit?"
["Why do we trade our land for one warmed by another sun? Who, in exile from his country, has also fled from himself?" — Horace, Od., ii. 16, 18.]

If a man does not first unload himself, and his mind, of the burden he finds himself carrying, motion will only make it press harder and sit heavier — just as a ship's cargo is less troublesome when it is fixed and settled in place. You do more harm than good to a sick man by moving him from place to place; you fix and entrench his disease by motion, as stakes are driven deeper and more firmly into the earth by being worked up and down in the spot where they're meant to stand. So it isn't enough to remove yourself from the public; it isn't enough to change the soil — a man must flee the popular habits that have taken root in his soul, must withdraw and come home to himself:
"Rupi jam vincula, dicas Nam luctata canis nodum arripit; attamen illi, Quum fugit, a collo trahitur pars longa catenae."
["You may say, 'I have broken my chains' — but a dog, after a long struggle, may snap the knot and still drag a long piece of the chain from its collar as it runs." — Persius, Sat., v. 158.]
We still carry our fetters along with us. It is no real freedom — we still glance back at what we have left behind us; the imagination is still full of it:

"Nisi purgatum est pectus, quae praelia nobis Atque pericula tunc ingratis insinuandum? Quantae conscindunt hominem cupedinis acres Sollicitum curae? quantique perinde timores? Quidve superbia, spurcitia, ac petulantia, quantas Efficiunt clades? quid luxus desidiesque?"

["But unless the mind is purified, what inner battles and dangers we then incur in spite of ourselves! How many bitter anxieties, how many fears follow on unbridled passion! What ruin pride, lust, and petulant anger work on us! What evils luxury and sloth bring!" — Lucretius, v. 4.]
Our disease lies in the mind, which cannot escape from itself;
"In culpa est animus, qui se non effugit unquam," — Horace, Ep., i. 14, 13.
and so it must be called home and confined to itself: that is the true solitude, and it can be enjoyed even in populous cities and in the courts of kings — though more comfortably apart.

Now, since we intend to live alone and to do without all manner of social commerce, let us arrange things so that our contentment depends wholly on ourselves. Let us dissolve all the bonds that tie us to others; let us secure from ourselves the ability to live alone in good earnest, and to live at our ease too.

When Stilpo had escaped the burning of his town, where he lost his wife, his children, and his goods, Demetrius Poliorcetes, seeing him appear undisturbed amid such a ruin of his country, asked him whether he had suffered no loss. Stilpo answered, No; and that, thank God, nothing of his had been lost. This was also what the philosopher Antisthenes meant when he said wryly that "a man should furnish himself with such things as would float, and that could escape the storm with their owner." And indeed a wise man never loses anything if he has himself. When the city of Nola was destroyed by the barbarians, Paulinus, who was bishop of the place, having lost everything he had and being himself a prisoner, prayed like this: "O Lord, keep me from feeling this loss; for you know that they have not yet touched anything of what is truly mine." The riches that made him rich and the goods that made him good were still intact. This is what it is to choose treasures that can defend themselves from plunder and violence, and to hide them in a place no one can enter and that can only be betrayed by ourselves. Wives, children, goods are to be had, and especially health, by those who can get them; but we are not to set our hearts on them so far that our happiness depends on them. We must reserve a back-shop, wholly our own and entirely free, in which to set up our true liberty, our chief solitude and retreat. There we are mostly to keep our own company, and so privately that no foreign acquaintance or commerce is admitted; there to laugh and to talk as if without wife, children, goods, retinue, or attendance — so that when it falls out that we must lose any or all of them, it will be no new thing for us to be without them. We have a mind pliable enough in itself to be company; it has what is needed to attack and defend, to receive and to give. Let us not, then, fear that we shall languish in this solitude under a dreary emptiness.
"In solis sis tibi turba locis."
["In solitude, be a crowd to yourself." — Tibullus, vi. 13. 12.]

Virtue is satisfied with herself, without discipline, without speeches, without effects. Of our ordinary actions there is not one in a thousand that really concerns us. The man you see scrambling up the ruins of that wall, in a fury and transported, with so many musket shots aimed at him; and the other, scarred all over, pale and faint with hunger, yet resolved to die rather than open the gates to him — do you think they are there for their own sake? No: they are there perhaps for someone they never saw, who never gives a thought to their pains and danger but lounges meanwhile in sloth and pleasure. And that drooling, bleary-eyed, slovenly fellow you see coming out of his study after midnight — do you think he has been poring over books to learn how to be a better, wiser, more contented man? Nothing of the sort. He will end his days at it, but he will teach posterity the metre of Plautus' verses and the right spelling of a Latin word. Who is it that does not willingly trade his health, his rest, and his very life for reputation and glory — the most useless, frivolous, false coin that circulates among us? Our own death does not trouble and terrify us enough; let us, on top of it, take on those of our wives, our children, our family. Our own affairs don't give us anxiety enough; let us take on those of our neighbours and friends, the better to wreck and torment ourselves:
"Vah! quemquamne hominem in animum instituere, aut Parare, quod sit carius, quam ipse est sibi?"
["Ah! can any man set up in his mind, or fix on, something dearer to him than he is to himself?" — Terence, Adelph., i. I, 13.]

Solitude seems to me to wear its best face for those who have already spent their most active and flourishing years in the world's service, after the example of Thales. We have lived enough for others; let us at least live out the small remnant of life for ourselves. Let us now draw in our thoughts and intentions to ourselves, to our own ease and rest. It is no light thing to make a safe retreat; it will be enough for us to do this without mixing in other enterprises. Since God gives us leave to arrange our departure, let us pack our bags, take leave in good time of the company, and untangle ourselves from those violent demands that pull us elsewhere and separate us from ourselves.

We must break the knot of our obligations, however strong; from now on we may love this thing or that, but marry nothing except ourselves. That is to say: let everything else be our own, but not so attached and so close that it cannot be torn off without flaying us or tearing out part of our whole. The greatest thing in the world is for a man to know that he is his own. It is time to wean ourselves from society when we can no longer add anything to it; whoever is not in a condition to lend must forbid himself to borrow. Our forces are beginning to fail; let us call them in and concentrate them in and for ourselves. Let whoever can cast off within himself, and dissolve, the offices of friendship and company, do so. In this decline of nature that makes him useless, burdensome, and a nuisance to others, let him take care not to be useless, burdensome, and a nuisance to himself. Let him soothe and care for himself, and above all govern himself with such reverence for his reason and conscience that he is ashamed to take a false step in their presence:
"Rarum est enim, ut satis se quisque vereatur."
["For it is rare that men feel enough respect and reverence for themselves." — Quintilian, x. 7.]

Socrates says that boys should have themselves instructed, grown men should exercise themselves in doing well, and old men should withdraw from all civil and military employments, living as they choose, without obligation to any office. Some temperaments are more suited to these counsels of retirement than others. People of soft and slow apprehension, of a tender will and affection, not easily put to work — among whom I count myself, both by nature and by reflection — will take to this advice more readily than active, busy souls, who embrace everything, throw themselves into everything, are hot for everything, offering and giving themselves up to every occasion. We are to make use of these accidental, external commodities so far as they please us, but by no means to lay our principal foundation on them; that is not a real one; neither nature nor reason allows it. Why, then, should we, against their laws, enslave our own contentment to another's power? To anticipate as well the accidents of fortune — to deprive ourselves of the conveniences we have in our own power, as some have done out of devotion and certain philosophers by reasoning; to be one's own servant, to lie hard, to put out one's own eyes, to throw one's wealth into the river, to go in search of grief; some aiming through this life's misery at bliss in another, others by laying themselves low to avoid the danger of falling — all such things are acts of an excessive virtue. The toughest and most resolute natures make even their seclusion glorious and exemplary:

"Tuta et parvula laudo, Quum res deficiunt, satis inter vilia fortis Verum, ubi quid melius contingit et unctius, idem Hos sapere et solos aio bene vivere, quorum Conspicitur nitidis fundata pecunia villis."

["When means run short, I praise a safe and modest condition, content with little; but when things grow better and richer, I say all the same that only those are wise and live well whose invested money shows in handsome villas." — Horace, Ep., i. 15, 42.]

A good deal less would do for me. It is enough for me, under fortune's favour, to prepare myself for her disgrace, and, while I am at ease, to picture to myself, as far as imagination can stretch, the trouble to come — as we do in jousts and tournaments, where we play at war in the deepest calm of peace. I do not think Arcesilaus the philosopher any less temperate and virtuous for the fact that he was known to use gold and silver vessels when his fortune allowed; indeed I think better of him than if he had denied himself what he used with liberality and moderation. I can see the utmost limits of natural necessity; and when I see a poor man begging at my door, often more cheerful and healthier than I am, I put myself in his place and try to fit my mind to his manner. Running through other examples in the same way, even when I picture death, poverty, contempt, and sickness at my heels, I easily resolve not to be alarmed, since someone less than I bears them so patiently; and I won't believe that a smaller understanding can do more than a greater, or that the effects of precept cannot rise as high as those of habit. And knowing how uncertain the duration of these accidental conveniences is, I never forget, in the height of all my enjoyments, to make it my chief prayer to Almighty God that He will be pleased to make me content with myself and with the condition I am in. I see young men, very gay and lively, who nevertheless keep a stock of pills in their trunk at home, ready when a cold comes — which they fear the less because they think they have a remedy on hand. Everyone should do the same; and if, moreover, they find themselves prone to some more violent disease, they should provide themselves with medicines that can numb and deaden the affected part.

The occupation a man chooses for such a life should be neither laborious nor unpleasant; otherwise there is no point in retiring at all. And that depends on each person's taste and temperament. Mine has no kind of liking for husbandry, and those who do love it ought to apply themselves to it in moderation:
["I try to make circumstances submit to me, not myself to circumstances." — Horace, Ep., i. i, 19.]

Husbandry is otherwise a very servile employment, as Sallust calls it; though some parts of it are more excusable than the rest — like the care of gardens, which Xenophon credits to Cyrus. A middle ground can be found between the sordid, low application, full of perpetual anxiety, that you see in men who make it their whole business and study, and the dull, extreme negligence that lets everything go to ruin, as you see in others:
"Democriti pecus edit agellos Cultaque, dum peregre est animus sine corpore velox."
["Democritus' cattle eat his corn and trample his fields, while his soaring mind ranges abroad without the body." — Horace, Ep., i, 12, 12.]

But let us hear what advice the younger Pliny gives his friend Caninius Rufus on the subject of solitude: "I advise you, in the full and plentiful retirement you have, to leave the care of husbandry to your labourers, and to give yourself up to the study of letters, and to draw from it something that may be entirely and absolutely your own." By which he means reputation — like Cicero, who says he would use his solitude and retirement from public affairs to acquire by his writings an immortal life:
"Usque adeone Scire tuum, nihil est, nisi te scire hoc, sciat alter?"
["Is your knowledge worth nothing at all, unless someone else knows that you know it?" — Persius, Sat., i. 23.]

It seems only reasonable, when a man talks of retiring from the world, that he should look entirely out of it. These men do it only by halves: they plan well enough for themselves for the time when they will no longer be in it, but they still mean to gather the fruits of that plan from the world after they have left it — which is a ridiculous contradiction.

The imagination of those who seek solitude out of devotion, filling their hopes and their courage with the certainty of divine promises in the other life, is far more rationally grounded. They set before themselves God, an object infinite in goodness and power; there the soul has, at full liberty, the means to satisfy her desires; afflictions and sufferings turn to their advantage, since they are borne for the acquisition of eternal health and joy; death is to be wished for and longed for as the passage to so perfect a condition; the severity of the rules they impose on themselves is soon softened by habit, and all their carnal appetites baffled and subdued by being refused indulgence and food — for these appetites are sustained only by use and exercise. This single goal of another, happily immortal life is what really deserves that we should give up the pleasures and conveniences of this one; and whoever can really and steadily kindle his soul with the heat of this living faith and hope builds for himself in solitude a more delightful and luxurious life than any other.

Neither the end, then, nor the means of Pliny's advice please me, for we often jump out of the frying-pan into the fire. This book-occupation is as wearing as any other, and as great an enemy to health, which ought to be the first consideration; nor should a man let himself be lured by the pleasure of it, which is the same kind of pleasure that ruins the frugal, the greedy, the voluptuous, and the ambitious.

["This plodding occupation of books is as painful as any other, and as great an enemy to health, which ought principally to be considered. And a man should not let himself be inveigled by the pleasure he takes in them." — Florio, edit. 1613, p. 122.]

The sages warn us often enough to beware the treachery of our desires, and to distinguish true and entire pleasures from those that are mixed up and complicated with greater pain. For most of our pleasures, they say, coax and caress us only to strangle us, like those thieves the Egyptians called Philistae. If the headache came before the drunkenness, we would be careful about drinking too much; but pleasure, to fool us, marches in front and hides her train. Books are pleasant; but if, by over-studying, we damage our health and ruin our good humour — the best parts we have — then let us give it up. I, for my part, am one of those who think no fruit drawn from books can make up for so great a loss. As men who have long felt themselves weakened by illness finally give themselves up to the mercy of medicine and submit to certain rules of living they are never afterwards to break, so the man who retires, tired and disgusted with the common way of life, should model this new life he is entering by the rules of reason, and set it up and establish it by deliberate thought and reflection. He should take leave of all kinds of labour, whatever advantage they may promise, and in general shake off the passions that disturb the peace of body and soul, and then choose the way that best suits his own temper:
"Unusquisque sua noverit ire via."

In husbandry, in study, in hunting, and in every other pursuit, we are to go to the utmost limits of pleasure, but to take care against going further, where trouble begins to mix in with it. We are to keep only as much activity as is needed to keep us in breath and to defend us from the inconveniences of the other extreme — dull, stupid laziness. There are sterile, knotty branches of knowledge, hammered out chiefly for the crowd; let them be left to those who are engaged in the world's service. For myself, I care for no books except either those that are pleasant and easy, to amuse me, or those that comfort me and instruct me how to regulate my life and my death:
"Tacitum sylvas inter reptare salubres, Curantem, quidquid dignum sapienti bonoque est."
["Silently wandering among the healthy groves, attending to whatever is worthy of a wise and good man." — Horace, Ep., i. 4, 4.]

Wiser men, with great strength and vigour of soul, may set themselves a wholly spiritual rest; but for me, who have a very ordinary soul, it is absolutely necessary to support myself with bodily comforts. And since age has of late deprived me of the pleasures that were more agreeable to me, I instruct and sharpen my appetite for those that remain, which suit this new stage. We should hold on with all our force, both hands and teeth, to the use of the pleasures of life that the years, one after another, snatch from us:
"Carpamus dulcia; nostrum est, Quod vivis; cinis, et manes, et fabula fies."
["Let us gather life's sweets — what you have while you live is yours. Soon you will be ashes, a ghost, a story." — Persius, Sat., v. 151.]

Now, as to the end that Pliny and Cicero set before us — glory — it is infinitely far from my account. Ambition is, of all dispositions, the most contrary to solitude; glory and rest are things that simply cannot live in the same place. As far as I can see, these men have only their arms and legs out of the crowd; their soul and intention remain confined behind it more than ever:
"Tun', vetule, auriculis alienis colligis escas?"
["Do you, then, old man, gather food for others' ears?" — Persius, Sat., i. 22.]

they have only stepped back to take a better leap, and with a stronger motion to plunge into the crowd again. Do you want to see how short they fall? Let us set against them the advice of two philosophers from two very different sects, writing — the one to Idomeneus, the other to Lucilius, their friends — urging them to retire into solitude from worldly honours and affairs. "You have," they say, "so far lived swimming and floating; come now and die in port. You have given the first part of your life to the light; give what remains to the shade. It is impossible to give up business unless you also give up its fruit; so disengage yourselves from all concern for fame and glory. The brilliance of your past actions risks following you into your most private retreat and giving you too much light. Give up, along with the other pleasures, the one that comes from another man's approval; and as for your knowledge and gifts, don't worry about them — they will not lose their effect provided you yourselves are the better for them. Remember the man who, asked why he took such pains in an art that could be appreciated by only a few, replied: 'A few are enough for me; one is enough; none would still be enough.' He spoke truly: you and a companion are theatre enough for one another, or you are enough for yourself. Let the people be one to you, and be one to the whole people. It is an unworthy ambition to want to draw glory from one's idleness and privacy. You should do as the hunted beasts do, who efface their tracks at the entrance to their den. You are no longer to concern yourself with how the world talks of you, but how you are to talk to yourself. Retire into yourself — but first prepare yourself there to receive yourself. It would be folly to trust yourself in your own hands if you can't govern yourself. A man can come to grief alone as well as in company. Until you have made yourself into someone before whom you would not dare to slip, until you have a sense of shame and respect for yourself,
"Obversentur species honestae animo;"
["Let honest images be ever present to the mind." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 22.]

keep continually before your imagination Cato, Phocion, and Aristides, in whose presence even fools would hide their faults; make them the controllers of all your intentions. Should those intentions stray from virtue, your respect for these men will put you right; they will keep you on the path of being contented with yourself, of borrowing nothing from anyone but yourself, of holding and fixing your soul on certain and limited thoughts in which she can take pleasure, and, having understood the true and real goods — which men enjoy the more, the more they understand them — of resting satisfied, without any desire to prolong life or name." This is the precept of the true and natural philosophy, not of a boastful, chattering philosophy like the other two.
